documents.title: David Thompson's Field Notes, June 1811
documents.transcription: Wednesday, June 22, 1811. A fine day. At 8 AM we proceeded on our voyage down the Columbia River. The current was very strong with many rapids. The river was full of large stones which made the navigation very dangerous. At 2 PM we came to a very bad rapid about half a mile in length - the water was dashing over rocks with great fury. We were obliged to unload and carry everything over the rocks, a portage of about 300 yards. The men were very tired.
documents.originalText: Wednesday 22nd June 1811. A fine day. At 8 AM proceeded on our voyage down the Columbia River. The current very strong with many rapids. The River full of large stones which render the navigation very dangerous. At 2 PM came to a very bad rapid about half a mile in length - the water dashing over rocks with great fury. We were obliged to unload and carry everything over the rocks, a portage of about 300 yards. The men much fatigued.

documents.title: Samuel Hearne's Journey to the Coppermine River, July 1771
documents.transcription: At one in the morning of July 14th, we arrived at the Coppermine River, at a part where it is about thirty yards wide and shallow. The Indians began to search for copper and were rewarded by finding several pieces of ore. Some pieces weighed more than four pounds. But the Indians would not give themselves the trouble of carrying this metal with them. I therefore took possession of such pieces as I found convenient to transport.
documents.originalText: At one in the morning of the fourteenth, we arrived at the Copper-mine River, at a part where it is about thirty yards wide, and shallow. The Indians began to search for copper, and were rewarded by finding several pieces of ore. Some pieces weigh'd upward of four pounds. But the Indians would not give themselves the trouble of carrying this metal with them. I therefore took possession of such pieces as I found convenient to transport.

documents.title: York Factory Trade Record, 1780
documents.transcription: August 1780. Total beaver pelts received this season: 34,567. Total Indigenous traders: 437 individuals from various nations. Goods traded: 234 guns, 4,890 lbs of gunpowder, 389 blankets, 567 brass kettles, 2,340 lbs of tobacco, and various other items. Noted that the 'Pedlars' from Canada [North West Company] have established posts inland and are intercepting our trade. I recommend the Company consider building posts in the interior.
documents.originalText: August 1780. Total beaver received this season: 34,567 Made Beaver. Total Indians traded with: 437 individuals from various nations. Goods dispensed: 234 guns, 4,890 lbs gunpowder, 389 blankets, 567 brass kettles, 2,340 lbs tobacco, sundry other articles. Noted that the Pedlars from Canada [North West Company] have established posts inland and are intercepting our trade. Recommend the Company consider building posts in the interior.

documents.title: Letter from Matonabbee to Samuel Hearne, 1772
documents.transcription: To my friend Samuel Hearne - The winter has been hard and game has been scarce. My people need ammunition and tobacco. The river routes are opening. I will bring my people to trade at your new house on the Saskatchewan River [Cumberland House]. I ask that you trade fairly as you promised. The Cree and Chipewyan must have peace to use these hunting lands. I will speak for my people. Your friend, Matonabbee.
documents.originalText: To my Friend Samuel Hearne - The winter has been hard and game scarce. My people need ammunition and tobacco. The river routes are opening. I will bring my people to trade at your new house on the Saskatchewan [Cumberland House]. I ask that you trade fairly as you promised. The Cree and Chipewyan must have peace to use these hunting lands. I will speak for my people. Your friend, Matonabbee.

documents.title: Alexander Mackenzie at Fort Fork, 1793
documents.transcription: Having assembled the men, I stated my determination to reach the Pacific Ocean by way of the Peace River and whatever waters might present themselves. I asked who would volunteer to accompany me on this voyage of discovery. All stepped forward without hesitation. The dangers are many - rapids, hostile tribes, starvation in unknown lands. Yet the glory of finding a route to the Western Sea spurred them on. We depart tomorrow with high spirits.

documents.title: Alexander Mackenzie's Rock Inscription at Bella Coola, July 1793
documents.transcription: Alexander Mackenzie, from Canada, by land, 22nd July 1793
documents.originalText: Alex Mackenzie from Canada by land 22d July 1793

documents.title: Alexander Mackenzie Crossing the Rocky Mountains, June 1793
documents.transcription: The navigation of this river is absolutely impracticable, even for canoes, in its present state. We continued our toilsome progress, overloaded as many of us were with two bags apiece. This work was so difficult that a third of our crew were left behind, and we did not expect they could join us before morning. The men were in a state of discontent which approached mutiny, and I could not help but acknowledge that their fatigue was excessive.
documents.originalText: The navigation of this river is absolutely impracticable, even for canoes, in its present state. We continued our toilsome progress, over-laden, as many of us were, with two bags apiece. This work was so toilsome that a third of our number were left behind, and we did not expect they could join us before morning. The men were in a state of discontent which approached to mutiny, and I could not but acknowledge that their fatigue was excessive.

documents.title: Peter Fidler Recording Saukamappee's Oral Histories, Winter 1792-1793
documents.transcription: Saukamappee, an aged Piikani (Peigan) elder, gave me the following account: In his young days, the Cree came to their lands to make peace and hunt buffalo together. The Cree had iron weapons and some guns from the Hudson's Bay Company traders. The Shoshone Indians to the south had horses, but the Piikani had never seen these wonderful animals. When the Shoshone rode down upon them on these great creatures, they fled in terror, thinking the horse and rider were one being. But the Cree with their guns stood and fought. The sound of the gun and the death it brought from a distance amazed both the Piikani and their enemies. After many battles, they drove the Shoshone people south and took their horses for themselves. Then the Piikani became the strongest people of the plains.
documents.originalText: Saukamappee, an aged Indian of the Piegon [Piegan/Piikani] tribe, gave me the following account: In his young days, the Nahathaway [Cree] came to their lands to make peace and hunt buffalo together. The Nahathaway had iron weapons and some guns from the Bay men. The Snake [Shoshone] Indians to the south had horses, but we had never seen these wonderful animals. When the Snake rode down upon us on these great creatures, we fled in terror, for we thought the horse and rider were one being. But the Nahathaway with their guns stood and fought. The sound of the gun and the death it brought from afar amazed both us and our enemies. After many battles, we drove the Snake people south and took their horses for ourselves. Then we became the strongest people of the plains.

documents.title: James Knight on Thanadelthur, York Factory, 1715
documents.transcription: This woman has conducted herself with such courage, resolution, and extraordinary fortitude that she has gained the admiration of all. She has undertaken to make peace between the Chipewyan and the Cree, two Nations at deadly enmity. When the parties met in suspicion and anger, she went boldly between them, speaking to them for hours until both sides agreed to peace. She is the chief promoter and active force in this reconciliation. I never saw a more clear-headed person than this woman. Should she succeed in bringing the Chipewyan to trade at York Factory, it will prove the foundation of much profit to the Company.
documents.originalText: This slave woman has conducted herself with such courage, resolution, and extraordinary fortitude that she has gained the admiration of all. She has undertaken to make peace between the Chipewyan and the Cree, two Nations at deadly enmity. When the parties met in suspicion and anger, she went boldly between them, haranguing them for hours until both sides agreed to peace. She is the chief promoter and actress in this reconciliation. I never saw a more clear-headed person than this woman. Should she succeed in bringing the Chipewyan to trade at York Factory, it will prove the foundation of much profit to the Company.

documents.title: David Thompson's References to Charlotte Small, 1799-1811
documents.transcription: My wife and three children accompanied me on this survey. Charlotte's skill with languages proved invaluable in speaking with the Kootenay peoples. At the difficult crossing of the Athabasca Pass, she managed the horses and supplies while I took observations. I am most fortunate in my partner, who bears hardship without complaint and maintains our children's welfare in the most trying circumstances. Her understanding of Indigenous customs has prevented misunderstandings that might have proved fatal.

documents.title: Samuel Hearne on Matonabbee's Leadership, 1770-1772
documents.transcription: I was now convinced that Matonabbee was right when he told me that I should never reach my destination with only a party of men. Women, said he, were made for labor; one of them can carry or haul as much as two men can do. They pitch our tents, make and mend our clothing, keep us warm at night; and in fact, there is no such thing as traveling any considerable distance in this country without their assistance. Matonabbee himself had seven wives, all of whom performed their share of the work. Under his direction, with proper supplies of women to make snowshoes and clothing and to carry baggage, I succeeded in reaching the Coppermine River and the sea beyond.

documents.title: Simon Fraser Navigating the Fraser River Canyon, June 1808
documents.transcription: This morning we proceeded onwards. The rapids were extremely dangerous and the Indigenous peoples urged us not to continue by water but to follow the trail over the mountain. However, we embarked. I have been for a long period in the Rocky Mountains, but have never seen anything like this country. We had to pass where no human being should venture. Yet in those places there is a regular footpath impressed upon the very rocks by frequent traveling. Besides this, steps are formed like a ladder by poles hanging to one another and crossed by pieces of timber. At one spot we were obliged to slide down a rock that was almost perpendicular, holding a small cord fastened above. The situation is dangerous in the extreme.
documents.originalText: This morning we proceeded onwards. The rapids were extremely dangerous and the natives urged us not to continue by water but to follow the trail over the mountain. However, we embarked. I have been for a long period in the Rocky Mountains, but have never seen anything like this country. We had to pass where no human being should venture. Yet in those places there is a regular footpath impressed upon the very rocks by frequent traveling over them. Besides this, steps are formed like a ladder by poles hanging to one another and crossed by pieces of timber. At one spot we were obliged to slide down a rock that was almost perpendicular, holding a small cord fastened above. The situation is dangerous in the extreme.

documents.title: Dr. John Rae's Report on Franklin Expedition Relics, 1854
documents.transcription: From the Inuit I learned that about four years ago, a party of white men, about forty in number, were seen traveling southward near the mouth of a large river. They were dragging boats and sledges. None of them could speak the Inuit language well enough to be understood. They were very thin and appeared to be in great distress. Later that season, but before the ice broke up, the bodies of some thirty people were discovered on the mainland, and five on an island nearby. Some of the bodies had been mutilated and had been used for food. The Inuit had in their possession many articles which had belonged to the lost expedition.
documents.originalText: From the Inuit I learned that about four winters past a party of white men, amounting to about forty, were seen traveling southward near the estuary of a large river. They were dragging boats and sledges. None of them could speak the Inuit language well enough to be understood. They were very thin and appeared to be in great distress. Later that season, but previous to the breaking up of the ice, the bodies of some thirty persons were discovered on the continent, and five on an island near it. Some of the bodies had been sadly mutilated and had been used as articles of food. The Inuit had in their possession many articles which had belonged to the lost expedition.

documents.title: Champlain's Account of the Founding of Quebec, July 1608
documents.transcription: The 3rd of July, I arrived at Quebec, where I immediately set to work at constructing habitations. At this place, I found the water of the river very good and the land rich... I caused the brush wood to be cut down for making our habitation, which had three buildings of two stories... The store-house was six fathoms long and three wide, with a fine cellar six feet high. Around the habitation I had a gallery made... I had a dove-cote made, and raised there were doves. Our gardens also flourished well. There are many good things to hope for from this land.

documents.title: Champlain's Description of Hochelaga and the St. Lawrence, 1611
documents.transcription: The river is most agreeable and abounds with fish of many kinds. On both sides of it are meadows and forests of fine tall trees. It is a country so pleasant and fruitful that it is a pity to see it lying neglected... The Indians call this place where we made our settlement Hochelaga. They showed me maps of the country made of bark, and explained the routes by which to travel to distant lands.

documents.title: Letter from Champlain to the King of France on New France, 1618
documents.transcription: Sire, Among all the useful and necessary arts, that of navigation has always seemed to me to hold the first rank... The new lands which I have discovered contain many natural riches waiting to be developed for the glory of God and the benefit of France. The great river of Canada leads to a vast country where the trade in furs promises great wealth. I beseech Your Majesty to support the establishment of a permanent colony...

documents.title: Cartier's Account of First Contact at Gaspé, July 1534
documents.transcription: On the 24th of said month, we had a cross made thirty feet high, which was put together in the presence of many of them on the point at the entrance to the harbour... The chief, Donnacona, came to parley with us, accompanied by three of his sons. After he had finished a long speech, pointing to the cross, he made us a sign that all this land was his, and that we ought not to have set up this cross without his permission...

documents.title: Cartier's Description of Stadacona and Hochelaga, October 1535
documents.transcription: We arrived at Hochelaga, where we found about a thousand persons, both men, women and children, who gave us as good a welcome as ever father gave to his son... The town is circular and is completely enclosed by a wooden palisade... There are some fifty houses, each about fifty or more paces in length and twelve to fifteen in width. They sleep on great pieces of bark on raised platforms, and have fish hanging from the roof.

documents.title: Cartier's Report on Scurvy and Indigenous Medicine, Winter 1535-1536
documents.transcription: By the middle of February, out of 110 men that we were, there were not ten in good health... Some lost all their strength and could not stand on their feet. Then their legs became swollen and puffed up, and as black as coal... Their gums rotted and the flesh fell away to the roots of the teeth, which nearly all fell out. A native showed us a tree called Annedda [white cedar] and how to grind the bark and leaves and boil all in water... God granted such a cure that if all the physicians of Louvain and Montpellier had been there with all the drugs of Alexandria, they would not have done so much in one year as this tree did in six days.

documents.title: La Salle's Claim of Louisiana at the Mississippi Delta, April 1682
documents.transcription: On the ninth day of April, in the year 1682, I, René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, in virtue of His Majesty's commission, which I hold in my hand, and which may be seen by all whom it may concern, have taken, and do now take, in the name of His Majesty and of his successors to the crown, possession of this country of Louisiana, the seas, harbors, ports, bays, adjacent straits, and all the nations, peoples, provinces, cities, towns, villages, mines, minerals, fisheries, streams, and rivers... from the mouth of the great river St. Louis, otherwise called the Ohio, as also along the river Colbert, or Mississippi...

documents.title: Letter from La Salle to Governor Frontenac on Mississippi Exploration, 1681
documents.transcription: Monsieur, I have now descended the great Mississippi to its mouth and have seen the vast extent of territory it drains. This river is the key to the continent. Whoever controls it commands commerce between the northern lakes and the southern seas. I have established Fort Crèvecoeur on the Illinois River, and propose to establish forts at strategic points along the Mississippi to secure this vital waterway for France...

documents.title: Henri Joutel's Account of La Salle's Final Expedition, 1687
documents.transcription: M. de La Salle had continued to struggle with misfortune. Our colony at Fort Saint Louis was reduced by disease and desertion. Food was scarce, and the men grew rebellious. On March 19th, near the Trinity River, the Sieur de La Salle went to search for provisions with a small party. Some of the men, driven to desperation, conspired against him. Duhaut and his confederates fell upon M. de La Salle and murdered him... Thus perished one of the greatest men of his age, who had discovered and explored more of this continent than any other.

documents.title: Tyrrell's Journal of the Barren Lands Expedition, July 1893
documents.transcription: July 12th - We have now entered the true Barren Lands. The last of the timber has disappeared behind us, and before us stretches an endless sea of tundra, broken only by scattered boulders and the silver thread of streams leading northward. Today we sighted a great herd of caribou, numbering perhaps ten thousand animals, streaming across our path. The Chipewyan guides assure us that such sights were common in their fathers' time...

documents.title: Tyrrell's Discovery of the Dinosaur Bone Beds, September 1884
documents.transcription: While conducting a geological survey along the Red Deer River, in the badlands of Alberta, I came upon an extraordinary deposit of fossilized bones of great antiquity. Protruding from the eroded bank of the river was what I believed to be the skull of a large dinosaurian creature. The specimen, later examined by experts, proved to be a previously unknown species of carnivorous dinosaur. The formation appears to contain many more such fossils...

documents.title: Letter from Tyrrell on the Geological Survey of the Klondike, 1898
documents.transcription: The gold deposits of the Klondike are truly remarkable in their extent and richness. Our surveys indicate that the gold-bearing gravels stretch for many miles along the creeks flowing into the Yukon River. The formation of these deposits dates to the Pleistocene era, when glacial action concentrated gold from the surrounding bedrock. I estimate that the total value of gold remaining in these fields exceeds many millions of dollars...

documents.title: Back's Journal of the Great Fish River Expedition, July 1834
documents.transcription: July 28th - After weeks of portages and rapids, we have at last reached the great river which the Indians call Thleweechodezeth, meaning 'Great Fish River.' It flows through country of unspeakable desolation, yet possessing a savage grandeur all its own. The river falls over a series of tremendous cataracts, through which we must carry our boats. The men are exhausted, but their spirits remain high...

documents.title: Back's Account of Wintering at Fort Reliance, 1833-1834
documents.transcription: The winter at Fort Reliance has tested us all severely. The thermometer has fallen to sixty degrees below zero, and at such temperatures the spirit in the instruments freezes solid. We have survived on caribou meat procured by the hunters and fish from the lake. The aurora borealis has provided nightly spectacles of extraordinary beauty, great curtains of light dancing across the heavens. Despite our hardships, I have used this time to gather astronomical observations and chart the surrounding territory...

documents.title: Letter from Back to the Admiralty on Franklin Relief, 1836
documents.transcription: My Lords, I have the honor to report on the expedition to relieve Captain John Ross, which, though he was fortunately rescued before our arrival, succeeded in accomplishing a complete survey of the Great Fish River to its outlet in the frozen sea. The journey was attended with extreme hardship. We traversed 7,500 miles by canoe and on foot, descending 83 rapids and making numerous portages. I am confident that this river offers no practical passage to the Northwest...

documents.title: Fidler's Survey Journal of the Athabasca Country, 1791
documents.transcription: December 15th - Travelled NW over frozen lakes and portages. The cold is intense, the thermometer showing 40 below zero. My Chipewyan guides move with remarkable speed on their snowshoes. I have been taking careful astronomical observations at each camp, fixing our position by the stars. Today we passed through country rich with beaver signs. The mountains to the west are now clearly visible, great snow-covered peaks that the natives call the 'Shining Mountains.'

documents.title: Fidler's Account of Living with the Peigan, 1792-1793
documents.transcription: I have now spent a full winter among the Peigan nation, learning their language and customs. Their knowledge of the land is profound - every hill and stream has a name and story. The old men tell of their fathers' battles and hunts, of the coming of the horse which transformed their way of life. I have recorded their accounts of the mountains and rivers to the west, making sketches of the lands they describe. The chief, Old Swan, has shown me great kindness...

documents.title: Fidler's Report on the Red River Settlement Survey, 1814
documents.transcription: I have completed the survey of lots along the Red and Assiniboine Rivers for Lord Selkirk's settlement. Each lot measures 10 chains in width along the river front, extending back two miles into the prairie. The soil is black and deep, well suited for agriculture. However, the Métis population views these surveys with suspicion, claiming that the land belongs to them by right of their mothers' people. The situation is tense, and I fear trouble may come...

documents.title: Turnor's Instructions to the Hudson's Bay Company, 1778
documents.transcription: Gentlemen, I beg leave to represent to your Honours the absolute necessity of training your servants in the science of surveying and astronomical observation. At present, your maps of the interior are largely guesswork, based on rough estimates of distance and direction. With proper instruments and instruction, we might produce accurate charts that would give the Company a great advantage over its rivals. I propose to establish a school of practical surveying...

documents.title: Turnor's Journal of the Survey to Lake Athabasca, 1790
documents.transcription: June 28th - We have at last reached the great Lake Athabasca, having travelled over 1,000 miles from Hudson Bay. I have taken observations at 47 stations along our route, each position fixed by lunar distances and meridian altitudes of the sun. My apprentices Fidler and David Thompson have proven apt pupils. The Canadian pedlars have established posts here and trade extensively with the Chipewyan. We must extend our operations into this country or lose it entirely...

documents.title: Turnor's Map and Report on the Churchill River System, 1792
documents.transcription: I have the honour to present my survey of the Churchill River from its mouth at Hudson Bay to its sources near Île-à-la-Crosse. This river, which the natives call Missinipi, offers the most direct route to the Athabasca country. I have marked 156 portages along its course, noting the length and difficulty of each. The accompanying map shows the river's true course for the first time, correcting the many errors in previous charts...

documents.title: Norton's Journal at Prince of Wales Fort, 1762
documents.transcription: The trade this season has been considerable, with upwards of 50 canoes arriving from the interior. The Northern Indians bring the finest furs, particularly marten and beaver. I have encouraged them to bring word of the copper mines their ancestors knew, and several chiefs have promised to guide an expedition. The stone fort is now nearly complete, a formidable structure that will secure our presence on this coast for generations...

documents.title: Norton's Instructions to Samuel Hearne, December 1770
documents.transcription: Mr. Hearne, You are hereby ordered to proceed overland to the Northern Ocean, in company with the Indian leader Matonabbee, whose wisdom and experience in travel I have the utmost confidence in. You are to take particular note of all rivers, lakes, and mountains, and to discover the latitude and longitude of the copper mines. You must conduct yourself with courtesy to all natives you encounter, remembering that our trade depends upon their goodwill...

documents.title: Norton's Trade Report to the London Committee, 1768
documents.transcription: Honourable Sirs, I have the pleasure to report that the trade at Churchill continues to prosper. This season we received 18,000 Made Beaver in furs, chiefly from the Chipewyan nation who travel great distances to trade with us. I recommend we encourage exploration inland to meet the natives closer to their hunting grounds, as our Canadian competitors are doing. The woman Thanadelthur, though now many years deceased, showed us what might be achieved through alliance with the Northern peoples...

documents.title: Stuart's Journal of the Journey Inland from York Factory, 1715-1716
documents.transcription: September 1715 - Set out from York Factory with the woman Thanadelthur and a party of Cree hunters. Our mission is to make peace between the Cree and the Northern Indians, and to encourage the latter to bring their furs to the Bay. The country is vast beyond imagining, endless forests and lakes stretching to the horizon. Thanadelthur serves as our interpreter and guide - without her knowledge we should be quite lost...

documents.title: Stuart's Report on Thanadelthur's Peace Mission, 1716
documents.transcription: When we at last encountered a band of Northern Indians, they were at first terrified of our Cree companions, their ancient enemies. But Thanadelthur harangued them for hours, speaking with such passion and eloquence that by nightfall they had agreed to smoke the peace pipe. She told them of the great advantages of trade with the English - of metal tools and cloth and kettles - and convinced them to send deputies to York Factory. It is no exaggeration to say that without this remarkable woman, our mission would have failed entirely...

documents.title: Stuart's Account of Trade Customs Among the Northern Indians, 1716
documents.transcription: The Northern Indians live by hunting caribou and trapping beaver. Their camps are small, each family moving frequently to follow the game. They make their canoes from birch bark, which they sew together with the roots of spruce trees. Before any trade can occur, there must be gift-giving and speeches. To rush into business without these ceremonies is considered the height of rudeness. I have learned to sit patiently while the pipe passes around the circle...

documents.title: La Pérouse's Account of the Attack on Prince of Wales Fort, August 1782
documents.transcription: August 8th, 1782 - At dawn we sighted the stone fortress of the English at the mouth of the Churchill River. My squadron consisted of three ships: the Sceptre, the Astree, and the Engageante, carrying 290 soldiers and sailors. The fortress appeared formidable, with massive walls and numerous cannon embrasures. However, upon landing our forces, we discovered the garrison numbered only 39 men under Governor Samuel Hearne. The Governor, recognizing the futility of resistance, requested terms of capitulation. I granted him honourable terms - the garrison would be released and transported to England, and the personal effects of the men would be respected...

documents.title: La Pérouse's Report on the Destruction of York Factory, August 1782
documents.transcription: Having secured Prince of Wales Fort, I proceeded to York Factory, the principal establishment of the Hudson's Bay Company. We arrived on August 24th and found the post defended by only a small garrison. The English had attempted to hide their most valuable stores, but we discovered great quantities of furs and trade goods. I ordered the buildings put to the torch, though I permitted the inhabitants to depart with provisions sufficient for their journey to the nearest English settlement. The destruction of these posts will deal a severe blow to English commerce...

documents.title: La Pérouse's Letter to the French Minister of Marine on the Hudson Bay Expedition, 1782
documents.transcription: Monseigneur, I have the honour to report the complete success of our expedition to Hudson Bay. We have destroyed the two principal English establishments - the stone fort at Churchill and the great trading post at York. The English trade in furs, which has enriched them for more than a century, will be severely disrupted. I must commend the conduct of the English Governor, Mr. Hearne, who behaved with great dignity under difficult circumstances. At his request, I returned to him his journals and scientific observations, which I judged to be of value to natural philosophy rather than to commerce...

documents.title: Samuel Hearne's Account of the French Capture, August 1782
documents.transcription: On the morning of August 8th, three French ships of war appeared before the fort. The Comte de La Pérouse commanded the squadron. With only 39 men fit for duty and no hope of relief, I had no choice but to seek terms. The French commander proved himself a man of honour. He permitted us to retain our personal belongings and promised safe passage to England. When I showed him my journals and maps from the Coppermine expedition, he expressed great interest and, to my surprise and gratitude, returned them to me, saying they belonged to science rather than to war...
